Normative data

Regression-based normative data adjusted for age, sex, and BMI are reported in the online supplemental material (Table S3 and Figure S2).

Discussion

This study adapted the Power of Food Scale (PFS) into Spanish. It evaluated its psychometric properties in a community sample of 810 adults in Argentina, to examine it as a transdiagnostic, dimensional measure of hedonic hunger across the severity continuum of binge-eating and eating-disorder symptoms. The evidence supports interpreting the total score: reliability was high, a bifactor structure with a dominant general factor fit well, and scores were strongly related to hedonic eating, binge-eating symptoms, and bulimic symptoms. Evidence for the subscales and for discriminant validity relative to a closely related measure was weaker, and clinical applications remain to be tested in clinical samples and against diagnostic interviews.

The three-factor model showed marginal fit in the confirmation subsample (CFI = .90, TLI = .88, RMSEA = .09). In contrast, the bifactor model fit well (CFI = .96, RMSEA = .07).

Because bifactor models tend to fit better than correlated-factors models, the bifactor indices are more informative: the general factor accounted for 71% of the common variance, ωH was .84, and ignoring the specific factors biased the general-factor loadings by only 5%. With these values, interpreting the total score as an essentially unidimensional index is justified (Reise et al., 2013; Rodriguez et al., 2016). By contrast, the specific factors explained little reliable variance once the general factor was controlled (ωS = .16, .23, and .31), so subscale scores should be interpreted with caution. This is consistent with prior validations supporting the three-factor structure (Aliasghari et al., 2020; Andreeva et al., 2019; Ribeiro et al., 2015; Torelli et al., 2022; Yoshikawa et al., 2012) while suggesting that most of the reliable variance in the PFS reflects a single dimension.

The subscale-level differences should be read in this light. Food Available and Food Present showed stronger associations with binge-eating severity (ε² = .375 and .329; AUC = .880 and .840) than Food Tasted (ε² = .101; AUC = .683). This pattern is compatible with the distinction between anticipatory wanting and consummatory liking (Berridge & Robinson, 2016). However, two measurement features offer an alternative reading: Food Tasted had the lowest reliability (ω = .76), and the items with the weakest loadings on the general factor (PFS9, PFS14, and PFS15; λ = .33-.45) attenuate its correlations. Food Tasted also retained the largest specific variance (ωS = .31), mainly through PFS9 (specific loading = .82), so a distinct taste-focus component may exist. However, this needs confirmation in independent samples before making differential interpretations.

Measurement invariance across biological sex was supported at the metric level, and the scalar model stayed within conventional thresholds (ΔCFI = -.003), so scores can be compared between women and men. Equivalence with the English-language original was not tested, and the adaptation relied on a single forward translation without independent backtranslation, so it remains unknown whether the Spanish and English versions are measurement-equivalent.

Convergent validity was strong: PFS scores correlated with hedonic eating (ρ = .59-.70), uncontrolled and emotional eating (ρ = .65 and .48), and bulimic symptoms (ρ = .62), and negatively with intuitive eating dimensions (ρ = -.17 to -.52), in line with accounts of hedonic hunger as sensitivity to food reward (Lowe & Butryn, 2007; McCrickerd & Forde, 2016) and with frameworks distinguishing cue-triggered motivation from interoceptive regulation (Dakin et al., 2025; Lopez & Cruz-Vespa, 2022). The near-zero association with cognitive restraint (ρ = .05) supports divergence from dietary restraint.

However, discriminant validity relative to the HEDO-Q was not established: latent correlations were high (r = .75 for Food Present and Food Tasted, .91 for Food Available), the HTMT was .89 (95% CI [.86, .92]), and the correlation between total scores corrected for attenuation was about .90. Although a correlation of 1 was statistically rejected, the two instruments overlap substantially and may largely index the same construct.

The strongest EDI-3 correlation emerged with the bulimia scale (ρ = .62), followed by drive for thinness (ρ = .36) and body dissatisfaction (ρ = .31). This graded pattern is consistent with the transdiagnostic view that hedonic responsiveness to food cues is most closely tied to loss-of-control eating, with smaller links to the weight-and shape-related symptom domains (Andrade et al., 2024; Andreeva et al., 2019; Di Segni et al., 2014; Franken, 2003; Lowe et al., 2009).

The PFS added a statistically significant but very small amount of explained variance in binge-eating severity beyond age, BMI, uncontrolled and emotional eating, and the HEDO-Q (ΔR² = .007), which, given the overlap with the HEDO-Q, indicates little unique predictive information. The two instruments are better seen as largely overlapping indicators of hedonic responsiveness than as measures of different constructs; comparing them directly in the same sample against prospective outcomes (e.g., loss-of-control eating, treatment engagement, weight change) is a priority for future research (Hilbert et al., 2022; Howard et al., 2021; Schreyer et al., 2023).

PFS scores increased across binge-eating severity groups with a large effect (ε² = .35), and discrimination of the high-severity group was good (AUC = .86, 95% CI [.82, .89]). A cutoff of 3.03 had sensitivity = .81 and specificity = .75 in the full sample, with nearly identical cross-validated values (.81 and .74), but a wide bootstrap interval (2.70-3.37).

These estimates should be treated as exploratory: both the PFS and the BES are self-reports, the BES severity groups were not validated against a diagnostic interview, and the EDI-based analysis (AUC = .77; cutoff = 2.77) used the 75th percentile of the same sample as the criterion, so it indicates only that higher PFS scores accompany higher symptom levels in this sample.

PFS scores predicted post-questionnaire hunger beyond baseline hunger and BMI, and this association was moderated by baseline hunger, consistent with an interactionist view in which hedonic responsiveness is expressed according to the momentary physiological context (Belfort-DeAguiar & Seo, 2018; Lowe & Butryn, 2007). Because food exposure was operationalized as questionnaire completion, hunger changes are descriptive indices rather than cue-reactivity outcomes.

PFS scores decreased with age and increased with BMI, and no sex differences emerged, in line with the invariance results indicating that scores can be compared between women and men. Associations with dieting status and hormonal cycle category agree with evidence that restriction increases food cue salience and that endocrine context influences hedonic responsiveness (Arnoni-Bauer et al., 2017; Hagan et al., 2003; Oswald et al., 2011; Swales et al., 2023).

Regression-based norms adjusted for age, sex, and BMI (Corvalán et al., 2026; Van der Elst, 2024) retained an age × sex interaction, indicating that the age-related decrease in PFS scores was attenuated in men. Given the convenience sampling strategy, these norms should be considered preliminary.

Constraints on Generality

The findings may not generalize beyond the studied sample. Participants were adults living in Argentina, recruited through social media using a snowball strategy; 73% were women, 40.1% had completed secondary education, and 34.1% had university education; race and ethnicity were not recorded, so we cannot examine how cultural, socioeconomic, and structural factors related to them shape hedonic hunger. The sample was non-clinical, and symptoms were self-reported, so the results may not apply to people with diagnosed eating disorders or to other Spanish-speaking countries, where food environments and language use differ. Replication in clinical samples, in other Spanish-speaking countries, and in more diverse samples is needed.

Limitations

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the adaptation relied on a single forward translation by a certified translator, reviewed by two authors, without independent back-translation, and we did not test measurement equivalence with the English-language original, so it remains unknown whether the two versions function equivalently. Second, the sample was non-clinical, predominantly female (73.3%), recruited online through snowball sampling, and limited to adults in Argentina, which restricts representativeness (see Constraints on Generality). Third, all measures were self-reports, open to social desirability, recall bias, and differences in introspective accuracy, and no diagnostic interview was used; the binge-eating severity groups and the eating-disorder composite therefore indicate symptom levels, not diagnoses, and the cutoffs derived from them are exploratory and imprecise.

Fourth, the criterion for the EDI-based analysis was the 75th percentile of the same sample, so it reflects relative standing in this sample rather than clinical risk. Fifth, the correlated three-factor model fit only marginally; the specific factors explained little reliable variance, and the PFS overlapped substantially with the HEDO-Q, limiting interpretation of subscale scores and the scale's distinctiveness from related measures. Sixth, we had no testretest data, so temporal stability is unknown. Seventh, food exposure was operationalized only as questionnaire completion rather than a standardized cue paradigm, so changes in hunger are descriptive indices, not cue-reactivity outcomes. Finally, the cross-sectional design precludes conclusions about predictive validity.

In sum, the Spanish-language PFS showed high reliability and a dominant general factor in Argentine adults, supporting the interpretation of its total score as an index of hedonic hunger that varies along the severity continuum of binge-eating and eating-disorder symptoms. Evidence for subscale scores and for discriminant validity relative to the HEDO-Q was limited. Future research should test the equivalence of the Spanish and English versions, examine the scale in clinical samples and against diagnostic interviews, include test-retest and prospective designs, and compare the PFS directly with the HEDO-Q (Burger & Stice, 2011; Lowe & Butryn, 2007). Online Supplemental Material

Method Translation and Adaptation Procedure

A certified public translator produced the initial Spanish version. Two authors then reviewed it against the English original for linguistic and conceptual equivalence and adjusted the wording. A focus group of 10 participants reviewed the adjusted version and commented on the clarity and comprehensibility of each item. Four external expert judges rated each item (Table S1), and the same two authors revised the two items with partial agreement (CVI = 0.50) based on the judges' comments, producing the final version. No independent back-translation was carried out, and equivalence with the English original was not tested empirically.

Results

Content validity

Content validity was evaluated through expert judgment using the Content Validity Index (CVI) calculated according to Lawshe's method (1975). Four independent experts assessed each item for semantic clarity and grammatical adequacy, as well as the appropriateness of its difficulty relative to the target population's educational and developmental level.

For semantic clarity and grammatical correctness, 13 of the 15 items had a CVI of 1.00, indicating full agreement among experts. Two items yielded a CVI of 0.50, reflecting partial agreement. Experts subsequently reviewed and refined these items based on qualitative feedback, making specific modifications to improve lexical precision and clarity.

Regarding item difficulty relative to the educational and developmental level of the Argentine adult population, all items had a CVI of 1.00, indicating unanimous expert agreement on the appropriateness of the language used. Overall, these findings support the content validity of the adapted scale and meet Lawshe's (1975) criteria. Detailed CVI values for each item are presented in Table S1.

Descriptive statistics and item analysis

Descriptive statistics were computed for all items of the Power of Food Scale, including means, medians, standard deviations, minimum and maximum values, and percentages of missing data. No missing responses were observed across items.

Item means ranged from 1.91 to 3.73 (SDs = 1.13-1.44), indicating moderate variability in endorsement levels. Item difficulty indices ranged from 22.84% to 68.22%, suggesting adequate variability across the response scale and no evidence of marked floor or ceiling effects.

Corrected item-total correlations ranged from .37 to .75, with most items showing moderate to high associations with the total score. One item (PFS9) presented a comparatively lower item-total correlation (r = .37), although it remained above conventional minimum thresholds for item retention. Overall, item-level results supported the scale's internal structure. Item-level descriptive statistics and psychometric indices are reported in Table S2, and inter-item associations are displayed in Figure S1C.

Reliability

Internal consistency was high for the total scale (Cronbach's α = .915; McDonald's ω = .934; split-half = .946). Reliability estimates for the subscales were also satisfactory:

Cronbach's α was .868 for Food Available, .854 for Food Present, and .778 for Food Tasted;

McDonald's ω was .873, .855, and .757; and split-half coefficients were .899, .856, and .783, respectively. The α and split-half coefficients were computed in the full sample (N = 810), and ω was computed from the CFA models in the second subsample (n = 405).

Structural validity Exploratory factor analysis

Structural validity was examined through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses; the confirmatory analyses are reported in the main manuscript. The sample was randomly divided into two equal subsamples (n = 405), and the exploratory factor analysis was run on the first one. Sampling adequacy was good (KMO = .93; item values .85-.95), and Bartlett's test of sphericity was significant, χ²(105) = 3,236.89, p < .001. Parallel analysis supported retaining three factors (observed eigenvalues of 6.55, 0.88, and 0.51 exceeded the simulated 0.43, 0.28, and 0.22, whereas the fourth, 0.16, fell below the simulated 0.19).

Exploratory factor analysis using maximum-likelihood extraction with oblimin rotation revealed a three-factor structure consistent with the scale's theoretical domains. The three factors accounted for 55.6% of the total variance (21.8%, 20.0%, and 13.7%), and communalities ranged from .36 to .86. Primary loadings ranged from .40 to .93, and three items (PFS3, PFS5, and PFS8) showed cross-loadings of at least .35 on a second factor.

Parallel analysis and exploratory factor loadings are shown in Figures S1A and S1B.

Figure S1. Exploratory Analyses of the Structure of the Power of Food Scale

Preliminary percentile-based reference values were calculated for the PFS total score.

Because PFS scores were associated with age, age-stratified percentile estimates were also examined. Median PFS scores were highest in the younger age groups and decreased progressively with increasing age. Specifically, the median (P50) was 2.87 in participants aged 18-25 years, 2.87 in those aged 26-35 years, 2.60 in those aged 36-45 years, 2.20 in those aged 46-60 years, and 2.13 in those aged 61 years and older. A similar age-related gradient was observed across the upper percentiles. These findings are consistent with the negative association observed between age and PFS scores and provide preliminary descriptive reference values for future research and potential clinical interpretation. Agestratified percentile estimates are reported in Table S3.

Regression-based normative data

Regression-based normative data were derived following the procedure described by Corvalán et al. (2026) and Van der Elst (2024). A linear regression model was estimated with PFS total scores as the outcome and age, biological sex, BMI, and their interactions as predictors, using stepwise backward elimination based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). The final model retained age (mean-centered), biological sex, BMI, and an age × sex interaction, and it met regression assumptions: homoscedasticity was supported (Breusch-Pagan: χ²(4) = 1.43, p = .232), and residuals showed adequate normality (KS = 0.044, p = .081).

Standardized residuals from the final model were converted to percentile ranks using the empirical cumulative distribution of the normative sample. The regression equation was:

PFS = 1.833 -0.022 × (age -39.00) -0.212 × (sex = male) + 0.037 × BMI + 0.012 × (age -39.00) × (sex = male). Figure S2 presents the diagnostic plots. Note. Upper right: the Q-Q plot of standardized residuals indicates approximate normality, with minor deviations at the tails that are expected in large samples and do not substantially affect coefficient estimation (Lumley et al., 2002).

Lower left: the Scale-Location plot shows a relatively flat trend, supporting homoscedasticity, consistent with the non-significant Breusch-Pagan test (χ²(4) = 1.43, p = .232). Lower right: the Residuals vs.

Leverage plot shows that no observations exceed Cook's distance thresholds, indicating no influential outliers. PFS = Power of Food Scale.

Convergent validity

Convergent validity was assessed by examining associations between PFS scores and related constructs. The PFS total score showed strong positive correlations with hedonic eating measures, including liking (ρ = .70), wanting (ρ = .70), and dyscontrol (ρ = .59).

Significant positive associations were also observed with uncontrolled eating (ρ = .65), emotional eating (ρ = .48), binge eating symptoms (ρ = .62), drive for thinness (ρ = .36).

Body dissatisfaction (ρ = .31). Negative correlations were observed with several intuitive eating dimensions, including reliance on hunger and satiety cues (ρ = -.37), body-food choice congruence (ρ = -.17), physical reasons for eating (ρ = -.36), and emotional reasons for eating (ρ = -.52). No significant association was found with cognitive restraint (ρ = .05, p = .198). Small but significant positive correlations were also observed with pre-exposure hunger (ρ = .22) and post-exposure hunger (ρ = .28). Subscale-level correlations revealed differential patterns across the three PFS dimensions (Table S6). The Food Available subscale showed the strongest associations with HEDO Dyscontrol (ρ = .62), emotional eating (ρ = .53), drive for thinness (ρ = .41), and cognitive restraint (ρ = .13). In contrast, these associations were weaker or non-significant for the Food Tasted subscale. Conversely, the Food Tasted subscale showed comparatively attenuated negative associations with intuitive eating dimensions. These differential patterns are compatible with partially distinct aspects of hedonic food motivation. However, given the low reliable specific variance of the subscales (see the main manuscript), they should be interpreted with caution. These findings support the scale's convergent validity. Full correlations are reported in Table 2 of the main manuscript.

Known-groups validity

Known-groups validity was assessed by comparing PFS scores across binge-eating severity groups derived from the Binge Eating Scale. Because the assumptions for parametric group comparisons were not met, we conducted non-parametric analyses. A Kruskal-Wallis test showed significant differences in PFS scores across BES severity groups (H = 280.40, p < .001).

Participants in the low binge-eating group had the lowest PFS scores (M = 2.20, SD = 0.69), followed by the moderate group (M = 2.81, SD = 0.72), whereas the high binge-eating group had the highest scores (M = 3.64, SD = 0.71). Post hoc comparisons indicated that all pairwise group differences were statistically significant after Bonferroni correction (all adjusted ps < .001). These findings suggest that the scale discriminates between groups that differ in binge-eating severity (Table S7).

Subscale-level analyses (Table S9A) revealed differential effect sizes across the three PFS dimensions. The Food Available subscale showed the largest effect (H = 304.81, p < .001, ε² = .375), followed by Food Present (H = 267.58, p < .001, ε² = .329), and Food Tasted (H = 83.19, p < .001, ε² = .101). All pairwise post hoc comparisons were significant for all three subscales (all adjusted ps < .001). Similarly, ROC analyses (Table S9B) indicated that the Food Available subscale showed the strongest discriminative performance (AUC = .880, 95% CI [.851, .909]), followed by Food Present (AUC = .840, 95% CI [.807, .872]), and Food Tasted (AUC = .683, 95% CI [.640, .725]). These differences should be interpreted with caution, because the subscales carry little reliable variance beyond the general factor (see the main manuscript)

Associations with sociodemographic variables and hunger measures

Associations between PFS scores and sociodemographic variables, including age, biological sex, body mass index (BMI), educational level, dieting status, and hormonal cycle phase, were examined. PFS scores were negatively associated with age (ρ = -.29, p < .001) and positively associated with BMI (ρ = .21, p < .001). Biological sex showed no significant differences (W = 68285, p = .177), and differences across educational levels did not reach conventional significance (H = 9.07, p = .060). In contrast, participants currently dieting showed significantly different PFS scores than those not dieting (W = 52378, p < .001), and significant differences also emerged across hormonal cycle categories (H = 73.64, p < .001).

Correlational and group comparison results are reported in Table S8. Consistent with the convergent validity analyses, PFS scores were positively associated with both pre-exposure eating severity (BES total score). Block 1 (age and BMI) accounted for 15.5% of the variance in BES scores (R² = .155). Adding uncontrolled eating, emotional eating (TFEQ), and the HEDO-Q total score in Block 2 produced a significant and substantial increase in explained variance (ΔR² = .467, ΔF = 336.86, p < .001), with the model accounting for 62.2% of the total variance. Adding PFS total scores in Block 3 yielded a statistically significant but very small increment in explained variance (ΔR² = .007, ΔF = 15.59, p < .001), with the overall model accounting for 62.9% of the variance. The standardized coefficient for PFS scores remained significant in the final model (B = 0.98, SE = 0.25, t = 3.95, p < .001; 95% CI [0.49, 1.46]), indicating a statistically significant but very small unique contribution of hedonic hunger beyond general eating dysregulation and hedonic overeating tendencies.

Trait-state and hedonic profile analyses

To further explore the theoretical relationship between trait hedonic responsiveness and momentary hunger, regression analyses were conducted predicting post-exposure hunger ratings. In a model controlling for baseline hunger and BMI, PFS scores significantly predicted post-exposure hunger (B = 3.29, SE = 0.56, t = 5.88, p < .001), whereas BMI did not significantly predict post-exposure hunger. Baseline hunger remained the strongest predictor (B = 0.80, SE = 0.02, t = 35.74, p < .001). An interaction model further showed a significant interaction between PFS scores and baseline hunger (B = 0.08, SE = 0.02, t = 3.41, p < .001), indicating that the association between trait hedonic responsiveness and postexposure hunger varied with baseline hunger.

Finally, exploratory analysis examining the joint pattern of PFS, binge eating severity, and hedonic eating dimensions showed that PFS scores were strongly associated with both binge eating severity (ρ = .63) and hedonic eating dimensions, especially liking (ρ = .70) and wanting (ρ = .70). The strongest association within this profile emerged between binge eating severity and hedonic dyscontrol (ρ = .72), suggesting a coherent hedonic vulnerability pattern across related constructs. Figure 3 of the main manuscript illustrates the distribution of PFS scores and their associations with binge eating severity.

The transition to the metric model resulted in a negligible change in fit (ΔCFI = -.002, ΔRMSEA = -.002, p = .069), supporting the equality of factor loadings across groups (metric invariance). The scalar model showed a further small decrease in fit (ΔCFI = -.003, ΔRMSEA = -.001), with the chi-square difference test reaching statistical significance (p = .002). Discrimination of binge-eating severity (exploratory)

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses evaluated the ability of PFS scores to discriminate the high binge-eating severity group (BES) from the rest of the sample. The PFS showed good discriminative performance, with an area under the curve (AUC) of .86 (bootstrap 95% CI [.82, .89]). The cutoff that maximized Youden's index was 3.03 (bootstrap 95% CI [2.70, 3.37]), yielding a sensitivity of .81 and a specificity of .75; in 10-fold crossvalidation, with the cutoff derived in the training folds, sensitivity was .81 and specificity .74 (Table S10).

A second, exploratory ROC analysis used scores at or above the 75th percentile of the

Eating Disorder Risk Composite (the raw sum of Drive for Thinness, Bulimia, and Body Dissatisfaction) in this sample as the criterion. The AUC was .77 (95% CI [.73, .81]), and the cutoff was 2.77 (bootstrap 95% CI [2.37, 3.17]), with an apparent sensitivity of .77 and specificity of .65 and cross-validated values of .77 and .65 (Table S10). Because the criterion was defined within the same sample, these values indicate only that higher PFS scores accompany higher symptom levels in this sample. Figure 2 in the main manuscript shows the ROC curves.

Participants were recruited through various social media platforms using a nonprobabilistic snowball sampling strategy. Participation was voluntary, unpaid, and optionally anonymous. Data collection took place between December 2025 and March 2026. Eligibility criteria included being a resident aged 18 or older and having Spanish as a native language.

was informed by the ITC guidelines for translating and adapting tests (International Test Commission, 2017). It was carried out under a license agreement with the copyright holder. The process had five steps: (a) a certified public translator produced a forward translation into Spanish; (b) two authors reviewed it for linguistic and conceptual equivalence with the original and adjusted the wording; (c) a focus group of 10 participants commented on item clarity and comprehensibility; (d) four external expert judges rated each item (see below); and (e) the same two authors revised the items according to the judges' ratings and comments, which produced the final version. No independent back-translation was carried out. Additional details are given in the online supplemental material.

Intuitive Eating Scale-2 (Tylka & Kroon Van Diest, 2013) assesses how much individuals regulate their eating based on internal hunger and satiety cues rather than external rules or emotional factors. The scale comprises four dimensions: Unconditional Permission to Eat, Eating for Physical Rather than Emotional Reasons, Reliance on Hunger and Satiety Cues, and Body-Food Choice Congruence. Items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), with higher scores indicating greater intuitive eating. Internal consistency of the Spanish version (Flores-Quijano et al., 2023) demonstrated good reliability in this sample.

Procedure

Participants were recruited through announcements disseminated on various social media platforms, including WhatsApp, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Reddit. Data were collected using SurveyMars, an online survey platform, through its free version. SurveyMars complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and implements data protection measures such as encrypting data at rest and in transit, access controls, and secure data storage in accordance with European data protection standards (SurveyMars, n.d.).

EDRC) in this sample. The EDRC is the sum of the raw scores of Drive for Thinness, Bulimia, and Body Dissatisfaction of the EDI-3; raw scores were used because standardized T-scores require normative tables. We chose cutoffs using Youden's index. To address optimism, we computed bootstrap 95% CIs (2,000 resamples) for the AUC and the cutoff, and 10-fold stratified cross-validated sensitivity and specificity (100 repetitions), deriving the cutoff only from the training folds. Incremental validity. A hierarchical regression predicted BES total scores in three blocks: age and BMI (Block 1); uncontrolled eating and emotional eating (TFEQ) and the HEDO-Q total score (Block 2); and the PFS total score (Block 3). The unique contribution of the PFS was evaluated using the change in R² and the F change at Block 3. Sociodemographic and hunger-related analyses. We examined associations of PFS scores with age, biological sex, BMI, educational level, dieting status, and hormonal cycle category using correlations or group comparisons, depending on the variable type. Linear regression tested whether PFS scores predicted post-exposure hunger controlling for baseline hunger and BMI, and an interaction model tested whether this association varied with baseline hunger. Associations among PFS scores, BES scores, and the HEDO-Q dimensions were examined to describe a hedonic profile.
